title: Connecting the Dots: A Series on Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS)
author: Elana
summary: A school educator examines how her school implements its Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS) framework and identifies a critical gap between having assessment structures and using data effectively. The school administers valid screeners three times per year and progress-monitors struggling students regularly, but teachers lack the data literacy to move beyond color-coded reports (red, yellow, green, blue) into substantive instructional analysis. The author illustrates this problem with fifth-grade beginning-of-year data showing roughly half of students below proficiency on oral reading fluency—a pattern that indicates a systemic Tier 1 instructional problem, not an individual intervention problem. When too many students need support, flooding Tier 3 with referrals overwhelms the system and fails the most struggling students who need it most. The more productive response is to first strengthen core instruction by asking whether the instructional design is working, what gaps exist, and what diagnostic data reveals about skill deficits. The piece argues that MTSS succeeds not through more data collection but through asking better questions of the data already in hand.
points: MTSS implementation often stalls at data collection rather than data use: schools gather valid assessment information but lack the data literacy to translate it into instructional decisions
When roughly half a class performs below proficiency, the problem is almost always a Tier 1 core instruction failure—not an individual student problem requiring individual intervention

Strengthening core instruction is more impactful than referring students to Tier 3 intervention: improving a whole-class instructional system reaches more students than the handful any intervention period can serve
quotes: Overall, school systems work hard, but not always effectively or efficiently.
What I find in places like my own school is that we have a few structures in place, like assessments, scheduling, and teams.
We haven’t yet figured out how to make sure each part of the skeleton has meat to its bones.
At my school, we give a valid and reliable screener three times a year.
We also have progress-monitoring tools that tell a more complete picture of how our students are doing on early literacy skills.
Students below proficiency and students who scored just above the proficiency cutoff are monitored every three weeks.
Students solidly at proficiency or above are monitored at the next benchmark period, and students well below the benchmark are monitored every other week.

One goal my school has identified, moving forward, is to progress-monitor our most struggling students weekly to increase the number of data points we have so we can adjust instruction earlier, if needed.
